translation:
So much research has been done on Kabirji's life story that a large volume could be written from it, and many scholars have written about him. The purpose of this piece is not to give his life story but to shed light on the image of him that is commonly current. Studying Kabir's character, one understands that he never falsely praised anyone, nor did he ever bow before falsehood. Kabirji, who grew up in an extremely poor family, had no means of livelihood other than the handloom. Every day he had to run the handloom, weave cloth, and sell it in the market, earning his living from whatever came of it. Kabirji never accepted gifts or money from anyone; he always earned his own living. Thus this extremely poor family remained poor throughout their lives.

Today, the images of Kabirji sold in the market by Kabirpanthis (followers of the Kabir path) and others show him seated on a golden throne, bearded, and clad in white garments. Kabirji never had such opulence in his life, nor did he ever ask his disciples for it. To depict Kabirji amid such luxury and indulgence is an insult to his principles and thought. One who never in his life had the chance to wear such opulent garments should never be depicted wearing them. The way he is shown in the image described above is actually Kabirji seated as one of the sixteen child-companions of the original Bansivat, appearing absorbed in contemplation and simple in bearing. That is his true character. Kabirji never accepted outward show or ostentation, so it is wrong to imagine him falsely as white-bearded or white-robed, seated upon a jewel-studded throne - such a depiction does not do justice to his character. We therefore hold the original Bansivat image to be the authentic one.
